A theme is a stylesheet, so the quality bar is mostly about restraint: few selectors, predictable tokens, and both modes treated as first-class.

## Start with tokens

Tokens are the contract between the theme and the app. A theme built from tokens survives component changes and usually survives app updates.

- Set only the tokens the design changes.
- Keep a comment or a grouping that explains the palette.
- Use the same accent family in both modes, adjusted for contrast.
- Treat `--ym-radius` and `--ym-shadow` as shape tokens, not as a place to patch individual components.

Reach for a component selector only when no token expresses the change.

## Design both modes

If the theme declares `"mode": "both"`, it is two themes sharing one name. Check both:

- body text on every surface, including hover and selected rows;
- muted and faint text, which are the first to disappear;
- borders on elevated cards;
- `--ym-on-accent` on the accent colour and its hover shade;
- danger, success and warning text on their backgrounds;
- focus rings and disabled controls.

If one mode cannot meet the bar, declare the single mode instead of shipping a weak second palette. A dark-only theme is honest; a theme that claims both and fails in light mode is not.

## Keep the palette coherent

- Derive hover and active shades from the surface colours, not from unrelated hex values.
- Keep the elevation order: rail, side, main, elevated, floating. A floating surface that is darker than the page looks inverted.
- Keep `--ym-accent-soft` translucent so it works over several surfaces.
- Pick `--ym-on-accent` deliberately. White is not always the accessible choice for a bright accent.

## Scope component CSS

Every plain rule should be scoped to the theme id:

```css
:root[data-yapmod-theme="my-theme"] .some-part {
  /* */
}
```

Unscoped rules keep applying after the user switches themes only if they remain in the document; they do not, because the whole style element is replaced. But unscoped rules are still risky inside the theme itself: they can hit elements you did not intend, and they make the theme harder to reason about.

Prefer one extra attribute of specificity over `!important`. Avoid styling the topbar drag region and dialog scroll locks; they are functional, not decorative.

## Be careful with assets

- Relative `url()` paths point at the Yapper page, not at the theme folder.
- Use a full `https:` address or a `data:` URI.
- Keep remote assets optional. A font or background that fails to load should not make the theme unusable.
- Do not use `@import`; the Community build rejects it, and a separate request delays first paint.
- Keep the stylesheet within the [size limit](/yapmod/docs/themes/manifest#limits).

## Match the manifest to reality

- The `id` is permanent enough to be a folder name. Choose it once.
- Keep `name`, `description` and `tags` accurate; they are what users search in the Community gallery.
- Update `version` when the visual result changes.
- Set `mode` to what you actually tested, not to what sounds more capable.
- Add a preview image that shows the theme in its primary mode.
- Include a license you have the right to use.

## Test the recovery path

A theme should be easy to leave:

1. Apply it.
2. Pick **Yapper's theme**. The normal look should return immediately.
3. Switch back. The theme should apply again without a restart.
4. Remove it. No attributes or style element should remain.

If a theme can only be escaped by deleting files, it is too invasive.

## Review before publishing

Before opening a pull request:

- test on a large and a narrow window;
- test with a long channel name and a long message;
- open settings, a dialog and a popover;
- check both modes (or the one declared mode);
- run the Community build with `pnpm check:web`;
- read [Submit a theme](/yapmod/docs/submit-a-theme) for the repository rules.

<Callout type="tip" title="Small beats clever">
A theme with twenty well-chosen token overrides is easier to review, easier to maintain and more likely to keep working than one with two hundred component selectors. If a rule fights the app, check whether a token already covers the case.
</Callout>
